Trying to Conceive

Male fertility supplements and food: what the evidence shows

Updated: November 4, 2026

Written and edited by BeMama Authors team: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

A bottle promising stronger sperm can feel like a practical step when pregnancy is taking longer than hoped. Nutrients matter, but taking extra is not the same as treating infertility. A useful decision considers the evidence for the actual product, any nutritional gap, affordable food choices and the need for timely assessment of both partners.

Sperm health is one part of fertility

Male factors can contribute alone or alongside a partner’s fertility condition. The proportion varies across populations; it is not helpful to turn an old prevalence estimate into blame. Sperm number, movement and shape are relevant, but a semen result does not by itself predict whether a pregnancy will happen. A low count can make conception harder without making natural conception impossible.

Age, smoking, some medicines, anabolic steroids, health conditions and certain workplace exposures can affect reproductive health. Nutrition is part of this picture, not an explanation for every abnormal result. A supplement cannot identify a hormonal problem, obstruction or other cause. Review relevant history and medicines with a clinician rather than stopping prescribed treatment yourself.

What male fertility supplements contain

Products sold as tablets, capsules, powders or liquids may combine zinc, selenium, folate, vitamins C and E, CoQ10, arginine, carnitine or omega-3 fats. Their amounts and combinations vary. The same ingredient name on two labels does not mean the products were studied in the same way or will have the same effects.

Some ingredients take part in normal cell function or antioxidant systems. That biological role does not prove that more improves fertility. A laboratory change, an animal experiment or a pregnancy testimonial is weaker evidence than a well-conducted human trial measuring pregnancy and live birth. A more expensive blend is not automatically more effective.

What current guidance and trials actually show

AUA/ASRM guidance describes the clinical usefulness of male fertility supplements as uncertain. WHO’s 2025 guideline could not recommend for or against antioxidants for infertile men with abnormal semen parameters. That uncertainty does not establish that every product works or that every possible use is ineffective; formulations, participants and meaningful outcomes differ.

In a large 2020 trial, folic acid plus zinc taken for six months did not improve live birth or most semen measures compared with placebo, and digestive side effects were more frequent. The 2025 SUMMER trial also found no improvement in ongoing pregnancy with one antioxidant blend alongside usual fertility care; a later treatment interval raised a possible harm signal. These findings do not test every supplement, and ongoing pregnancy is not the same outcome as live birth.

Treat a nutritional gap, not an advertising promise

A clinician or registered dietitian can review your usual meals, restrictions, health conditions and medicines to identify a likely deficiency or difficulty meeting needs. Testing is selected for the situation; a long commercial nutrient panel is not automatically necessary. Correcting a deficiency is a different goal from taking a fertility blend when nutritional needs are already met.

If a supplement is appropriate, agree on the ingredient, amount, reason, duration and review plan. Bring all labels, including multivitamins and sports products, so duplicate ingredients are counted. Feeling involved in the trying-to-conceive process matters, but you do not need to buy an unproven product to show commitment or support your partner.

Build a varied food pattern

Meals containing vegetables, fruit, whole grains, beans, nuts and suitable protein sources provide nutrients together with fibre and other useful food components. Choose unsaturated fats, such as olive oil, in place of some saturated fats rather than adding unlimited extra oil. A pattern you can afford and repeat is more useful than a restrictive list of supposed fertility superfoods.

Food research often measures semen quality or observes people who also differ in smoking, activity and health. These studies cannot promise that changing a menu will lead to pregnancy or protect a future child from every health problem. Eating well supports general health while fertility assessment and any indicated treatment continue.

Nuts: useful food, limited fertility conclusions

Unsalted walnuts or other tolerated nuts can be added to breakfast or used as a snack. Small trials in healthy young men eating Western-style diets found improvements in selected semen measures: one used 75 grams of walnuts daily for 12 weeks, and another used 60 grams of mixed nuts daily for 14 weeks. They did not establish that nuts increase pregnancy or live-birth rates in couples with infertility.

Those study amounts are not a required fertility dose and should not be described as one small handful. Choose portions that fit your appetite, energy needs and budget; nuts can replace another snack rather than simply adding more food. Avoid nuts you are allergic to. Brazil nuts contain particularly high selenium amounts, so eating many each day is not a safe way to imitate a supplement.

Include zinc-rich foods without megadoses

Meat, poultry, fish, well-cooked shellfish and fortified cereals provide zinc; beans, nuts, whole grains, eggs and dairy also contribute. Pumpkin seeds can be part of a varied pattern. For example, add beans to a grain bowl, have eggs with wholegrain toast or include a modest portion of meat or fish with vegetables. You do not need oysters or costly specialty foods.

Plant foods contain compounds that can reduce zinc absorption, so people with a restrictive or vegan diet may benefit from individual nutrition advice. This is not a reason to assume deficiency or start high-dose tablets. Too much zinc can cause stomach symptoms and, over time, low copper levels; it can also interfere with some antibiotics. A pharmacist can check the exact combination and timing.

Oily fish and other omega-3 sources

Salmon, sardines, trout and similar oily fish provide EPA and DHA omega-3 fats. As a general UK healthy-eating example, advice is at least two portions of fish weekly, including one oily portion, with a portion around 140 grams. Follow local species and contaminant advice; pregnancy guidance for the partner carrying a pregnancy can differ. Cook and store seafood safely and avoid foods that trigger your allergies.

Walnuts, chia and flax supply the plant omega-3 ALA, which the body converts to EPA and DHA only in limited amounts. Algal products can supply DHA, sometimes EPA, but a capsule is not automatically needed or proven to improve fertility. There is no established universal fish-oil fertility dose or six-month guarantee. Review supplements with a clinician, especially with anticoagulants; prescribed omega-3 treatment for another condition has a separate purpose.

Tomatoes and lycopene: keep the claim modest

Tomatoes are one source of lycopene and fit easily into meals as a sauce, soup or salad. Cooking tomatoes with a little olive oil is a practical meal option, not a treatment prescription. Other colourful vegetables and fruit add variety; they do not all contain the same pigment or the same nutrient amounts.

A small trial of a lycopene formulation in healthy men reported changes in some secondary sperm measures, but its main measure of motile sperm concentration did not improve significantly. That does not show that a serving of tomatoes treats infertility or increases live birth. Enjoy tomatoes as food without converting a capsule study into a food-dose promise.

Make fruit and vegetables a daily habit

Add a vegetable to lunch, include fruit at breakfast or keep frozen vegetables available for quick dinners. Fresh, frozen and suitable canned choices can all make variety easier. Fruit and vegetables provide nutrients such as folate and vitamin C, but a particular antioxidant list does not guarantee better sperm DNA or a healthier baby.

Portion targets vary by country and age. The UK’s five-a-day example means at least five 80-gram portions of fruit and vegetables in total, not five of each. There is no universal male-fertility rule requiring exactly two fruit and five vegetable servings. Build gradually toward local healthy-eating guidance and seek tailored advice if illness or dietary restrictions change what you can eat.

A realistic plan for meals and spending

Start with two or three repeatable changes: add beans or another protein source to lunch, include vegetables at the main meal, and swap a usual snack for fruit or a suitable portion of nuts. A meal might combine cooked salmon, vegetables and rice; a bean-and-vegetable dish is another option. These are examples for variety, not a prescribed menu or equivalent nutrient doses.

Keep a short record of food restrictions, supplements, medicines and questions for your appointment. Compare the ongoing cost of a blend with groceries or nutrition advice. If a clinician suggests an add-on, ask which outcome it might improve and when to review it. Choosing not to buy it is reasonable when the benefit remains uncertain.

Check product quality and possible reactions

A label should state every ingredient and amount per daily serving. Quality testing can help assess contents and contaminants, but a seal does not prove fertility benefit or personal safety. Regulation differs between countries. Avoid products promising to cure every cause of infertility, and do not combine several high-dose products because they are described as natural.

Food and supplements can cause allergic reactions. Call emergency services for suspected anaphylaxis, including sudden swelling of the lips, mouth, tongue or throat; breathing or swallowing difficulty; blue, grey or pale colour; sudden marked confusion, drowsiness or dizziness; or fainting with failure to wake. Any one can warrant help; a rash is not required. Use your prescribed adrenaline auto-injector and follow your emergency plan. For other new reactions, stop the suspected nonessential supplement and obtain professional advice.

Do not let a trial of supplements delay assessment

For regular unprotected intercourse without pregnancy, ASRM advises evaluation after 12 months when the partner providing eggs is under 35, or after six months at 35 or older. Above 40, seek advice sooner. Known sperm problems, irregular or absent periods, sexual difficulties or another relevant condition justify earlier assessment rather than waiting for a supplement course to finish.

Both partners should be assessed when applicable. A medical and reproductive history and semen analysis help guide next steps; an abnormal result may need repeat testing and specialist review. There is no guaranteed improvement date after changing diet. Continue sensible nutrition and health care together, without blaming yourself if conception requires treatment or takes longer than expected.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

Separate nutritional adequacy, semen measurements, pregnancy and live birth when interpreting evidence.

Use current fertility guidance and primary trials without turning research doses into a personal regimen.

Adapt ordinary food choices to allergies, medical needs, local guidance and affordability.

How BeMama can help

BeMama explains the full supplement-versus-food decision without endorsing a product or promising conception.

When to seek help

This article does not diagnose infertility or prescribe supplements. Review deficiencies, medicines and dietary restrictions with a qualified professional. Seek fertility assessment when indicated and emergency help for suspected anaphylaxis; follow your prescribed allergy action plan.

Evidence notes updated: November 4, 2026

Key takeaways

  • A better semen measurement does not necessarily mean more pregnancies or live births.
  • Treating a deficiency differs from taking an unproven fertility blend.
  • Nuts, zinc-rich foods, oily fish and varied produce can fit ordinary balanced meals.
  • Study amounts are not personal prescriptions, and more nutrients are not always safer.
  • Review medicines and supplements together and seek fertility assessment on time.

Frequently asked questions

What are male fertility supplements?

They are products containing nutrients or other ingredients marketed for sperm health or conception. Ingredients and doses vary, and their sale does not establish that they treat infertility.

Do they really work?

Evidence for meaningful fertility benefit remains uncertain. Large trials of particular products have not improved live birth or ongoing pregnancy. Some studies report semen changes, which are a different outcome.

Which vitamins improve male fertility?

There is no vitamin list guaranteed to improve fertility. Meet nutritional needs through a varied diet and correct a confirmed or likely deficiency with appropriate advice; avoid assuming that extra amounts help when needs are already met.

What foods should I choose?

Use a varied pattern with vegetables, fruit, whole grains, beans, tolerated nuts and suitable protein sources. Zinc-rich foods and oily fish can contribute nutrients, but no single food or menu guarantees conception.

How many walnuts should I eat?

Trials used measured amounts of 75 grams of walnuts for 12 weeks or 60 grams of mixed nuts for 14 weeks in healthy young men. These are research amounts, not a fertility prescription. Choose an appropriate portion and avoid nuts if allergic.

Should I take fish oil if I do not eat fish?

Not automatically. Review your overall diet and needs; plant ALA and algal DHA/EPA are different sources. A clinician or dietitian can help, but no universal fish-oil fertility regimen has been established.

Can supplements be harmful?

Yes. Excess zinc or selenium, overlapping ingredients and medicine interactions can cause problems. Quality seals do not eliminate risk. Review the full product list, and get emergency help for a suspected serious allergic reaction.

Should I wait three or six months before getting tested?

Do not postpone indicated assessment to finish a diet or supplement trial. Age, the time already spent trying and known health problems determine when to seek help; both partners may need evaluation.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
